name: Design a Content Moderation Pipeline
intent: Screen tens of millions of user uploads a day against known-bad lists, classifiers and human judgement, remove what breaks the rules, and be able to explain and reverse every decision.
codeTitle: a three-way triage with hash matching and a prioritised review queue
finalIntro: One photo uploaded by a user, from the first check to a decision that is recorded and can be appealed.
prompt: Design the moderation pipeline for a social app where users upload 50 million photos and videos a day. Illegal and abusive content must be kept off the platform, most uploads are fine and should appear at once, borderline cases need a human, and users who are wrongly punished must be able to appeal.
functional: Screen every upload before or soon after it is published
Block content that matches lists of known-bad material
Score the rest with classifiers, and act automatically only when the score is clear
Send uncertain items to human reviewers, most urgent first, within a deadline
Apply different rules in different countries
Let users appeal, and record every decision with its reason
nonFunctional: A normal upload is checked and visible in a couple of seconds
A hash lookup takes a few milliseconds, so it can run on every upload
Handle about 600 uploads per second on average and 2,000 at the peak
Severe content is reviewed within an hour, and ordinary reports within a day
Almost nothing that is allowed may be wrongly removed, and almost nothing severe may stay up
Every decision can be explained later, and reviewers are protected from harm

firstAttempt.text: Publish everything at once. Users report what they dislike, each report becomes a row in a table, and a team of moderators works through the table in the order the reports arrived, removing content by hand.
limits: Harmful content is visible until somebody reports it and a moderator gets to it, which can take days
Known illegal material that has been removed a thousand times is uploaded again and has to be found again
Moderators look at every report, but most reports are about harmless content, so their time is wasted
First come, first served means a severe report waits behind hundreds of trivial ones
One set of rules is applied everywhere, and there is no record of why anything was removed

steps.title: Check every upload against known-bad hashes first
steps.problem: A large share of the worst content is not new: it is the same file, or a lightly edited copy, that has been found and removed before, and waiting for a person to see it again is slow and harmful.
steps.fix: Before an upload is published, compute a fingerprint of it and look it up in lists of known-bad material, from the company's own past removals and from shared industry lists. An exact hash such as SHA-256 catches identical files. A perceptual hash, which stays similar when a picture is resized, cropped or recompressed, catches edited copies, by finding any stored hash within a small Hamming distance. The lookup runs against an in-memory index and takes a few milliseconds. A match blocks the upload and records the reason, with no person involved.
steps.tradeoff: It is nearly free, fast and has very few false positives when a match is exact, and it never forgets what was removed. It only finds what is already known. A perceptual match has a distance threshold that must be tuned, because a loose threshold starts to match innocent pictures, and a bad entry in a list blocks every copy of a harmless file.

steps.title: Score the rest with classifiers, and act only when sure
steps.problem: Most harmful content is new, and a model can look at 50 million uploads a day, but it is never certain, so one yes-or-no cut-off would either remove innocent content or let harm through.
steps.fix: Run classifiers for each kind of harm, such as nudity, violence, hate and spam, on the images, the video frames and the text. Each returns a score between 0 and 1. Two thresholds divide the scores into three bands: at or above the high threshold the content is removed automatically, below the low one it is published, and the band between goes to a person. Raising the high threshold means fewer wrongful removals (higher precision) but more work for people, and lowering the low threshold means fewer misses (higher recall) but more work for people too. The thresholds are set for each kind of harm from labelled samples, with a much stricter setting for the most severe categories.
steps.tradeoff: Almost all uploads are decided in milliseconds with no human, and the cost of the two kinds of error is placed on purpose. There is no setting without errors: the scores of harmful and harmless content overlap, so every choice trades wrongful removals against missed harm against reviewer workload.

steps.title: Put uncertain items in a priority queue with deadlines
steps.problem: A plain list of items for review is read in arrival order, so a child-safety report waits behind thousands of spam complaints, and nobody knows whether the team is falling behind.
steps.fix: Items for review go into a queue where each has a priority made from the severity of the suspected harm, the classifier score, how many people have seen it or reported it, and how long it has waited. Each priority class has a deadline: for example one hour for the most severe, 24 hours for ordinary reports. Reviewers pull the highest priority item next, and an item is locked to one reviewer while they work on it. When the queue grows faster than reviewers can empty it, the system sheds the least urgent work in a planned way, for example by publishing low-risk items without review and sampling them later, and it never drops the severe class. A decision service applies the reviewer's verdict to the content store.
steps.tradeoff: People spend their time on the cases that matter most and the deadlines are measurable. Low priority items can wait a very long time under heavy load, so they need an age boost or a fixed capacity share to avoid starving, and shedding means some harm stays up for longer on purpose.

steps.title: Apply the rules of each region as data
steps.problem: What is illegal or against policy differs by country, and a single global yes-or-no decision either removes lawful speech somewhere or leaves unlawful content visible somewhere else.
steps.fix: The classifiers and reviewers produce labels, such as 'graphic violence' or 'hate symbol', and not final verdicts. The decision service turns labels into actions with a versioned policy table: for each label and each region, one of allow, age-gate, reduce reach, hide in this country, or remove everywhere. Content hidden in one country is still stored, and the edge checks the viewer's country before it serves it. A policy change is a new table version that is tested in shadow mode on past decisions before it goes live, and every decision records which version it used.
steps.tradeoff: One piece of content can be treated correctly in each place, and a change in the law means a data change and not new code. The table needs legal and policy owners, the number of cases to test grows with the number of regions, and users can try to avoid a hide by changing their location.

steps.title: Allow appeals, and keep an audit trail for every decision
steps.problem: Every system makes mistakes, and without a way to challenge a decision wrongly punished users are stuck, while regulators and the team itself cannot tell why something was removed.
steps.fix: Each decision is written to an append-only log with the content id, the action, the label, the model version and score, the policy version, the reviewer or rule that decided and the time. A user who is told that content was removed is given the reason and an appeal button, and the appeal goes into the review queue as a new item, handled by a different reviewer than the first one. If the appeal wins, the content is restored and the original decision is marked as overturned in the log, which is how the real error rate is measured. The log is kept for the legal retention period, with access limited and recorded.
steps.tradeoff: Mistakes can be found, undone and counted, and the team can answer a regulator or a user with facts. The log holds sensitive material and grows with every decision, appeals add review work (a few percent of removals), and a restore must also undo the penalties and the notices that followed the removal.

steps.title: Measure the quality, and protect the reviewers
steps.problem: Reviewers see the worst content people upload, which damages them over time, and nobody knows whether the humans and the models are actually right.
steps.fix: Reviewers see images blurred or in grey-scale by default, with the sound off, and they open the full version only when needed. Their exposure is limited in the tool itself, for example a few hours a day, forced breaks and rotation to other work, with counselling support. For quality, a share of items is reviewed by two people, hidden test items with a known answer are mixed into the queue, and a sample of the automatic decisions is checked by people to measure the real precision and recall. Disagreement and drift raise an alert, and the labels from reviewers become the training data for the next model.
steps.tradeoff: It protects the people who do the hardest work, and gives real numbers to set the thresholds with. Limits on exposure mean more reviewers are needed for the same volume, double review and test items use part of the capacity, and measuring accuracy needs a sample large enough to be meaningful for rare categories.

failures.scenario: A new classifier version makes scores run higher
failures.impact: The same high threshold now removes many harmless posts, and the review queue overflows within hours.
failures.answer: A new model first runs in shadow mode on live traffic, and then at a small percentage with the share of auto-removals, the queue growth and the overturned-appeal rate watched against the old model. A jump beyond a limit triggers an alert and an automatic rollback, and thresholds are tied to the model version, so they are re-tuned for the new one.

failures.scenario: A viral event floods the system with reports
failures.impact: Reports and uploads about one event multiply tenfold, and the queue grows faster than reviewers can handle it.
failures.answer: Duplicate and near-duplicate items are grouped, so one decision covers a whole cluster. Priority puts severe items first and an age boost stops the low classes from waiting for ever. If the backlog still passes its limit, the lowest-risk items are published and sampled afterwards, and extra reviewers or a surge team are called in. The severe class is never shed.

failures.scenario: A wrong entry is added to the shared hash list
failures.impact: A harmless and very popular image matches, and it is blocked for millions of users in a few minutes.
failures.answer: Hash list updates are versioned and applied gradually. Every block records the list version and the entry, so the entry can be found and removed in seconds and the affected decisions can be listed and reversed in bulk. Entries that match unusually many different users are flagged for a human check before they are enforced.

failures.scenario: A decision is applied twice, or the content store is slow
failures.impact: A reviewer's verdict is retried and removes the content twice, sends the user two notices and counts two strikes.
failures.answer: Each decision has a unique id, and the decision service applies it once and records the outcome, so a retry returns the same result. The strike, the notice and the log entry are written together with the state change and sent out afterwards from an outbox, so none of them can happen without the others.

failures.scenario: A user keeps uploading the same banned content in new disguises
failures.impact: Small edits, such as a border, a mirror image or a filter, change the exact hash and get past the first check.
failures.answer: Perceptual hashes tolerate those edits, and the classifiers see the content itself. Once a person confirms the item, its hash goes into the known-bad list so the next copy is blocked in milliseconds. Repeat offenders are rate-limited and their uploads are routed to review first.

alternatives.title: When to check an upload

options.name: Before publishing (pre-moderation)
options.con: Everything waits for the check, and anything that needs a person is delayed

options.name: After publishing (post-moderation)
options.pro: Instant posting and a cheaper system
options.con: Harmful content is visible until it is caught

options.name: Hybrid by risk
options.pro: Fast checks block before publishing, and only the uncertain, low-risk items are checked afterwards
options.con: Two paths to run and a risk rule to maintain

alternatives.pick: A hybrid: hash and classifier checks run before publishing, and the review of low-risk uncertain items can follow it.

alternatives.title: Hash type for known content

options.name: Exact (cryptographic) hash
options.pro: No false matches, tiny and exact
options.con: One changed pixel or a recompression defeats it

options.name: Perceptual hash
options.con: A distance threshold to tune, and some false matches

alternatives.pick: Both: exact for a certain, instant block, and perceptual for edited copies with a tuned distance.

alternatives.title: Where the thresholds sit

options.name: One threshold for everything
options.con: Wrong for most categories, because the cost of a mistake differs

options.name: Per category, with a review band
options.pro: Strict for severe harm and forgiving for borderline content
options.con: More settings to tune and to monitor

alternatives.pick: Per category, with a review band sized to the capacity of the reviewers.

alternatives.title: Who reviews

options.name: In-house trained team
options.pro: Quality, context and control of the training
options.con: The most expensive way, and hard to scale for a surge

options.name: Outsourced vendors
options.pro: Flexible capacity and coverage in many languages
options.con: Less control over quality and over reviewer wellbeing

options.name: Crowd or community moderators
options.pro: Cheap and deep knowledge of the local context
options.con: Uneven quality, and not suitable for the most severe material

alternatives.pick: A trained core team for severe categories and appeals, with vendors for volume, all in the same tool and measured the same way.
